candidates.name: Go byte-valued strings and hexadecimal byte escapes
candidates.reason: Go's arbitrary-byte strings let a programmer combine readable ASCII with hexadecimal byte escapes and retrieve individual bytes without requiring the complete sequence to be Unicode.
candidates.application_scope: Readable byte sequences for mixed-encoding protocol or document data, plus individual byte access through indexing.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Ordinary source characters are UTF-8 encoded; high raw bytes need byte escapes, rune literals denote Unicode code points, and range iteration decodes runes rather than providing byte-wise traversal.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened official article is dated 23 October 2013 and directly explains arbitrary bytes, hexadecimal escapes and byte indexing.

raw_response:
I found four language designs relevant to readable raw bytes. All four were selected from the opened [Awesome Programming Languages catalogue](https://github.com/gendotnew/programming-languages) and then checked against their primary documentation. The first two have verified evidence before the 2014-06-04 cutoff; the other two are retained as later evidence.

1. **Go: byte-valued strings with explicit byte escapes.** [The official explanation](https://go.dev/blog/strings), dated 23 October 2013, shows that a string may contain arbitrary bytes, including invalid UTF-8, and that indexing retrieves individual bytes. This helps express a sequence such as "GET \xff" with readable ASCII and exact non-text bytes. **Transfer caveat:** ordinary source characters are UTF-8 encoded, rune literals denote code points, and range iteration decodes Unicode; a raw-byte API should preserve the distinction between byte indexing and Unicode iteration. **Date status: pre_decision.**

2. **OCaml 4.01: a matched pair of eight-bit character literals and string literals.** The archived [lexical reference](https://ocaml.org/manual/4.01/lex.html) gives single-quoted characters and double-quoted sequences the same numeric escapes, while the [value definitions](https://ocaml.org/manual/4.01/values.html) specify character values from 0 through 255. This suggests readable scalar notation such as 'A' or '\xFF' alongside a sequence such as "PDF\x00", without needing whole-sequence Unicode validation. **Transfer caveat:** the manual gives high characters an ISO-8859-1 interpretation; an encoding-neutral design should borrow the byte representation and syntax without importing that interpretation. The [manual index](https://ocaml.org/manual/4.01/index.html) is explicitly dated 12 September 2013. **Date status: pre_decision.**

3. **Python: explicit bytes literals separate from Unicode text.** The [lexical reference](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html) specifies b-prefixed literals, readable ASCII content, and explicit escapes for high bytes and NUL; the [binary-sequence reference](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html) distinguishes integer indexing from byte-sequence slicing. This helps make b"GET \xff" visibly different from a Unicode string while keeping each byte numerically accessible. **Transfer caveat:** b"A" remains a sequence; b"A"[0] yields an integer, so it does not supply a separate scalar byte-character literal. The successfully opened pages identify Python 3.15.2 and were updated on 20 November 2026; attempts to retrieve older 3.3.0 and 3.3 references failed. **Date status: post_decision; no pre-cutoff claim is made.**

4. **Nim: single-byte characters with byte-preserving strings and separate Unicode values.** The [official manual](https://nim-lang.github.io/Nim/manual.html) defines char as one byte, single-quoted character literals with numeric escapes, and strings whose UTF-8 convention is not enforced. This provides a coherent model for readable individual bytes and mixed binary sequences, with Rune and Unicode iteration available separately. **Transfer caveat:** a caller can still choose Unicode-oriented operations, so the byte-oriented contract must remain explicit. The opened manual was generated on 20 November 2026 and is linked from the Nim 2.4.3 documentation overview. **Date status: post_decision; no older version was verified.**

My translation of these examples is to give byte scalars and byte sequences an explicit representation, allow printable ASCII directly, preserve non-text values through numeric escapes, and make decoding into Unicode a separate operation. These are design precedents, not evidence of deployment or demonstrated usefulness for this particular problem.

Coverage limits: the search was restricted to permitted catalogues. A Rust catalogue page was rate-limited, its raw rendition was unavailable, and another Rust catalogue landing page did not expose its README body. Two non-catalogue bstr snippets appeared despite a catalogue-oriented query; neither was used as discovery or verification evidence, and bstr is not returned as a candidate.
